title: Ex 8.8 · Union distributes over intersection
prompt: Let $A$, $B$ and $C$ be any sets. Prove the distributive law $A \cup (B \cap C) = (A \cup B) \cap (A \cup C)$. Work one line at a time: unpack what it means for an element $x$ to be in the left side, rearrange that statement with a logic law, and repack it as membership in the right side.
answer_format: A chain of lines, each a set (like A ∪ (B ∩ C)) or a statement about an element x (like x ∈ A or x ∈ B). Each line must have exactly the same elements as the line before; start from the left side and end at the right side.
hints: Begin with x ∈ A ∪ (B ∩ C). By the definitions of ∪ and ∩ this says: x ∈ A, or (x ∈ B and x ∈ C).
Distribute the 'or' over the 'and': P ∨ (Q ∧ R) is the same as (P ∨ Q) ∧ (P ∨ R).
Now (x ∈ A or x ∈ B) is x ∈ A ∪ B, and (x ∈ A or x ∈ C) is x ∈ A ∪ C. Both hold, so x is in their intersection.
solution: Let $x$ be any element. By the definitions of union and intersection, $x \in A \cup (B \cap C)$ means $x \in A \lor (x \in B \land x \in C)$.
By the distributive law $P \lor (Q \land R) = (P \lor Q) \land (P \lor R)$, this is the same as $(x \in A \lor x \in B) \land (x \in A \lor x \in C)$.
That says $x \in A \cup B$ and $x \in A \cup C$, which means $x \in (A \cup B) \cap (A \cup C)$.
Each step was an equivalence, so the two sets have exactly the same elements: $A \cup (B \cap C) = (A \cup B) \cap (A \cup C)$. $\blacksquare$

reference.note: This exact exercise, restated in ProofLab's words. Uses Section 8.3 (proving A = B), the definitions of union, intersection and difference (Section 1.5) and the logic laws of Section 2.6.

x ∈ A ∪ B and x ∈ A ∪ C
